turns.question: Which supplements have good scientific evidence of benefit for generally healthy men around age 40?
turns.objective: Explain what the evidence shows: which supplements have good scientific evidence of benefit for generally healthy men around age 40
turns.config: searchBudget=6 spendLimit=500¢ stages=[GATHER, FILL_GAPS] outputTokens=8000 wordingCheck=true
turns.shown:
Supplements with good evidence for healthy men around 40 — Partly answered: 3 things it rests on aren't established.
Few supplements have good evidence of benefit for healthy men around 40 (the cited sources do not show: 40; the cited evidence is more tentative than this). Rests on findings that are not established: Creatine for training outcomes is the best supported, and prevention claims for the common supplements are unproven. The US Preventive Services Task Force recommends against beta carotene or vitamin E for preventing cardiovascular disease or cancer (the cited sources do not show: US Preventive Services Task Force; the cited evidence is more tentative than this). Only indicated, not established: It found the evidence insufficient for multivitamins and for single or paired nutrients. [1] VITAL is the largest trial of vitamin D and omega-3 in generally healthy people (the cited evidence is more tentative than this). It tested vitamin D3 at 2000 IU a day and marine omega-3 at 1 g a day (the cited sources do not show: 2000 IU, 1 g; the cited evidence is more tentative than this). Only indicated, not established: It enrolled men aged 50 or older and women aged 55 or older. That is older than your age group, so the results may not carry over to men around 40 (the cited sources do not show: 40). [29] [4] [5] [6] Only indicated, not established: Vitamin D did not lower the incidence of invasive cancer or cardiovascular events compared with placebo. [29] [4] [5] [6] Omega-3 did not lower the incidence of major cardiovascular events or cancer compared with placebo. Major cardiovascular events occurred in 386 people on omega-3 and 419 on placebo. A possible heart attack signal appeared in subgroups (the cited evidence is more tentative than this). The paper reports a suggestion of larger differences in heart attack risk among Black participants and those with low fish intake (the cited sources do not show: Black, larger differences in heart attack risk among Black participants and those with low fish intake). The authors note that some subgroup analyses rest on small numbers of events. Treat that signal as unconfirmed. [30] [31] [32] [6] Overall, the evidence does not support taking multivitamins, vitamin D or omega-3 to prevent heart disease or cancer in healthy men (the cited evidence is more tentative than this). Rests on findings that are not established: This is a judgment from the findings above, not a separate finding.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: USPSTF recommends against beta carotene or vitamin E for preventing cardiovascular disease or cancer. It finds the evidence insufficient for multivitamins and for single or paired nutrients.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Vitamin D did not significantly reduce major cardiovascular events or total cancer in VITAL. The trial population was older than 40.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Few supplements have good evidence of benefit for this group. Creatine for training outcomes is best supported. Prevention claims for multivitamins, vitamin D and omega-3 are unproven.

What I couldn't establish
- Other supplements (protein, magnesium, zinc, ashwagandha, testosterone boosters, probiotics) — not covered by my three searches, so I make no claim about them.
- Multivitamin effects on cognition or other outcomes (for example the COSMOS trial) — not searched.
- Evidence specific to men aged about 40 — the trials I found enrolled older adults or mixed ages, and I found no age-40 trials.
- Newer systematic reviews of creatine in middle-aged men — I relied on the 2017 position stand and a 2025 safety analysis.
- Whether VITAL findings apply to men around 40 — I found no trial of vitamin D or omega-3 for prevention limited to adults in their 40s. The VITAL results rest on participants aged 50 and older.
- Whether the USPSTF recommendation is still current — I did not run a new search on this. It still rests on the 2022 page.
